result_semantic_payload.summary: The delegated question asks for a reconstruction of the EDGE-GW latency timeline from the alert log and an assessment of what the records do and do not establish about causality between a maintenance drill and latency degradation/recovery. That reconstruction is NOT possible with the evidence reachable through the allowed read-only tools. The task contains exactly four files whose names match the question's premises (/monitor/latency-alerts.log, /change/maintenance-record.txt, /mail/oncall-handover.txt, /README.txt), but no tool exposed their contents: get_evidence returned null/empty content_preview at both 'digest' and 'preview' hydration levels, llm_summary/llm_description/initial_summary/initial_description are all null, md5 is empty, and there are 0 secondary analyses and 0 related-evidence links. The only facts actually observable are filesystem metadata (inode, size, mtime/ctime, is_deleted=0) and 8 timeline events consisting of one CREATED cluster and one MODIFIED cluster covering all four files. Consequently no EDGE-GW latency datapoint, no alert timestamp, no maintenance-drill window, and no recovery marker could be read, and no causal statement — in either direction — can be supported. What the record set DOES establish is limited to provenance/metadata: (a) the four artefacts coexist on the same filesystem and were created in a single instant (epoch 1790848014) and modified in a single instant (epoch 1737504000), i.e. their timestamps are degenerate and cannot be used to order the drill against the degradation; (b) the mtime (1737504000) precedes the recorded CREATED timestamp (1790848014) by ~5.3 years, which is internally inconsistent and indicates these are fabricated/fixture timestamps rather than forensic captures; (c) no file is deleted and no other file activity, logon, execution, registry or event-log evidence exists anywhere in the task. What the record set does NOT establish: that EDGE-GW ever degraded; that a maintenance drill occurred; that any alert fired; that latency recovered; that the drill temporally preceded, coincided with, or caused the degradation; and that the handover mail corroborates any of the above. A further structural limitation is that the delegated source scope 'windows' is not registered: get_task_context reports platforms=[] and source_scopes=[], so the Windows specialist profile (account usage, execution traces, persistence, device activity) has no backing source scope at all. The honest answer to the question is therefore a negative finding on evidence availability, with the caveat that a causality assessment cannot be rendered from metadata alone — even with content, co-timestamped files would not by themselves establish causation.

warnings: PRIMARY DELIVERABLE UNFULFILLED: the EDGE-GW latency timeline cannot be reconstructed because /monitor/latency-alerts.log content is not retrievable through any allowed tool. This result is a negative finding on evidence availability, not a substantive incident analysis.

The delegation names source scope 'windows' but the task registers no platforms and no source scopes (platforms=[], source_scopes=[]). The scope appears to be a mislabel; the task is a small generic-forensics file set, not a Windows image.

Do NOT treat the four co-timestamped files as evidence that the maintenance drill caused the latency degradation. The only observable relationship is identical degenerate timestamps, which is inconsistent (mtime precedes ctime by ~5.3 years) and cannot support any causal direction.

File content may well contain the full causal narrative — the files are non-empty (165-270 B) — so the negative finding reflects tooling/extraction failure, not necessarily an empty record set. Re-extraction is the highest-value next step.
